cards.explanation: The answer is neither of them. Jesus says, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him.” The disciples handed Him a two-option question, and He answered with a third door. I've been handed plenty of questions with no good choices, so I respect that move.

The answer is the light of the world. Jesus says, “While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” He says it right after talking about night coming, when no one can work. Light and night in the same breath, and it all fits. I know what a sliver of light means after my years in the dark of a junk drawer, friends.

The answer is True. Jesus tells the man to go wash in the Pool of Siloam, which means Sent. The man goes, washes and comes back seeing. He does just what Jesus told him to do, friends. He was blind from birth when he left, and he's seeing when he returns.

The answer is “I am the one.” While some say it's him and others say it's not, the man keeps saying, “I am the one.” He's got the best proof in the whole argument, because he's the guy. When everyone's debating who you are, it helps to just keep saying it, friends.

The answer is False. When the neighbors ask where Jesus is, the man answers, “I do not know…” He can tell them everything about what happened to his eyes, but not where Jesus has gone. I like how plainly he says it, friends.

The answer is a Sabbath. John 9:14 says the day Jesus made the mud and opened the man's eyes was a Sabbath. That's a small detail with big consequences, friends. The Pharisees pick it up in a hurry, as you'll see.
The answer is False. He doesn't refuse to tell the Pharisees. He says, “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and now I can see.” He gives them an answer right there, friends.

The answer is “How can a sinful man perform such signs?” Some Pharisees say Jesus is not from God, but others ask exactly that. It's a sharp question, because it points at what Jesus actually did. The Pharisees are split, friends, and it all starts with a Sabbath and some mud.

The answer is that he is a prophet. Asked what he says about Jesus, since it was his eyes that were opened, the man replies, “He is a prophet…” Earlier he said, “The man they call Jesus…” and now he says prophet. I think that's a step up, friends, and he says it out loud.

The answers are son and blind. His parents say, “We know he is our son…” and “…we know he was born blind.” Even with leaders breathing down their necks, those parts they say plainly. A parent knows their own, friends. It fits what the man himself says: “I was blind, but now I see!”
The answer is True. His parents say, “But how he can now see or who opened his eyes, we do not know.” They'll confirm he's their son and that he was born blind. Past that, friends, they stop.

The answer is that they are afraid of the Jews. The text says, “His parents said this because they were afraid of the Jews.” The Jews had already decided that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue. It's a pressure moment, friends, and I think anybody who's felt that knot in their stomach understands.

The answer is that they would be put out of the synagogue. John 9:22 says the Jews “…had already determined that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue.” Verse 23 says that was why his parents said, “He is old enough. Ask him.” That's the pressure they were under, friends.

The answer is “I was blind but now I see.” When the man is told Jesus is a sinner, he says, “Whether He is a sinner I do not know. There is one thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see!” He doesn't pretend to know more than he does. He stands on what he knows, friends, and nobody can argue him off it.

The answer is False. He doesn't walk through the story again. He says, “I already told you, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again?” Then he asks if they also want to become Jesus' disciples, friends.

The answer is disciples of Moses. The Jews say to the man, “You are His disciple; we are disciples of Moses.” Then they add, “We know that God spoke to Moses…” They put themselves on one side and the man on the other, friends.

The answer is False. Instead of backing down, the man says, “That is remarkable indeed!” Then he lays out his point: they don't know where Jesus is from, and yet He opened his eyes. A man who sat and begged is now out-arguing the experts, friends, and I'm here for it.

The answer is False. The man says, “Never before has anyone heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind.” He's telling them this has never been heard of, friends. It's the strongest evidence in the room, and he's wearing it.

The answer is God. The man says, “If this man were not from God, He could do no such thing.” That's the end of his argument, friends, and it's tight. He saw what happened, and he followed it to the only place it leads.

The answer is that they throw him out. Right after the man makes his case, they answer, “You were born in utter sin, and you are instructing us?” And they threw him out. It's a heavy moment, friends, and I think this one stings.

The answer is that he asks who the Son of Man is. He says, “Who is He, Sir? Tell me so that I may believe in Him.” He's ready to believe, friends, he just needs to know who. It's an honest question, and it gets an answer.
The answer is True. The man says, “Lord, I believe…” and he worshiped Jesus. He's the man who used to sit and beg, and now he worships Jesus, friends. What a turn.

The answer is blind. Jesus says, “For judgment I have come into this world, so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind.” And in this story we just watched a blind man see, friends. The words and the story line up.

The answer is “Are we blind too?” Some of the Pharisees with Jesus ask it right after He says that those who see may become blind. I think it's the kind of question people ask when a statement hits close to home, friends.

The answer is that their guilt remains. Jesus says, “If you were blind, you would not be guilty of sin. But since you claim you can see, your guilt remains.” He ties their guilt to their claim to see. It's a serious line, friends, and Jesus leaves it there.
